title: Bank loan demand weakens as lenders draw sharper lines between borrowers
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: US banks saw weaker demand for both business loans and home mortgages during the third quarter. The retreat in demand was broader than the change in approval standards. Domestic banks largely maintained their standards for lending to larger companies, tightened modestly for small firms, and tightened more broadly for commercial property. The October survey also identified borrowers moving in the opposite direction. Banks reported stronger demand from private equity funds and business credit intermediaries even as they tightened standards for those borrowers. Those differences matter for interpreting weak loan growth as evidence of weaker spending, tighter credit supply or a shift in where firms borrow.

The Board released the survey at 2 p.m. Eastern time on November 2. Officials sent the questionnaire on September 21 and requested responses by October 5. Sixty-one domestic banks and 18 US branches and agencies of foreign banks replied. Most questions ask about changes over the preceding three months, broadly the third quarter. The chart-data file labels this round 2026:4 by survey period. Its quarterly financial information therefore predates the November release. The percentages count banks answering each question. Net tightening subtracts the share easing from the share tightening, while net stronger demand subtracts the share reporting weaker interest from the share reporting stronger interest. A reading within five percentage points of zero is described as basically unchanged. Neither balance measures the number or dollar value of loans affected.

For commercial and industrial credit, the October balance for tighter standards was 1.7% for large and middle-market firms and 5.1% for smaller firms. The split uses annual sales of $50 million. Four of 60 banks tightened for the larger group and three eased. Four of 59 tightened for the smaller group and only one eased. Much of the apparent distinction in the labels therefore comes from just two fewer lenders easing and the different denominators. Loan pricing tells a different part of the story. On net, 15.0% of banks narrowed spreads over funding costs for larger borrowers, and 6.8% narrowed them for smaller borrowers. Risk premiums nevertheless increased on riskier loans in both groups, and smaller firms also faced tighter collateral requirements and more use of rate floors. A bank can therefore offer competitive terms on approved loans while becoming more selective about the risks it accepts.

The larger change in the business data was on the borrower side. The domestic balance reporting stronger demand for large and middle-market loans fell from +16.1% in the July survey to −11.7% in October. For small firms it moved from +3.6% to −11.9%. Banks with weaker demand cited reduced spending on plant or equipment and customers finding more attractive finance elsewhere. These imply different paths for total business investment. A firm that drops an investment project needs less finance overall, whereas one that moves to another lender may still undertake the project. Foreign branches and agencies offer a useful comparison. All 18 reported unchanged C&I standards. Of 17 answering the demand question, four reported stronger demand and none reported weaker demand. Differences in the borrowers served prevent this from resolving which explanation dominates.

Commercial property showed tighter supply alongside weaker demand across all three domestic categories. Construction and land development had the largest net tightening at 15.5%, with net demand at −25.9%. The corresponding pairs were +8.8% and −10.5% for loans on nonfarm nonresidential property, and +8.8% and −22.8% for multifamily property. In the July survey the standards balances had all been negative. The reversal indicates that more banks began moving standards in a restrictive direction. It says little about the absolute difficulty of borrowing, which also depends on earlier rounds of tightening and the borrower’s characteristics. The foreign panel reported both tighter standards and stronger demand for CRE overall, further caution against treating the domestic result as a market-wide quantity change.

Home-purchase mortgage demand weakened across every category surveyed. Approval standards generally remained stable, eased for both qualified and nonqualified jumbo mortgages and tightened for subprime mortgages. The subprime demand balance reached −40%, but only ten banks answered that question and four reported weaker demand. Home-equity lines of credit saw little net change on either side. Consumer credit also split by use. Domestic banks’ balance for stronger card demand was +10.2%, compared with −12.5% for auto credit. Broad approval standards were largely steady, while banks tightened certain contract terms, including card limits and minimum required auto credit scores.

The card questions covering the preceding year show why an unchanged aggregate standard can hide substantial differences across households. Banks became more willing to approve prime and super-prime applicants and less willing to approve subprime applicants, principally at smaller banks. For the near-prime group six banks were more willing and six less willing. For subprime applicants, 30 of the 56 respondents said they did not originate such loans. The change among active lenders thus concerns a narrowly served group. Banks most frequently cited changes in spending needs in response to prices faced by households when explaining upward pressure on card demand. The responses identify lenders’ perceptions of their customers’ motives, rather than actual spending or repayment outcomes.

The special questions on nondepository financial institutions bring the lending network into view. Domestic banks tightened standards for all five borrower groups. Ten of 52 tightened for private equity funds and two eased, yet eight of 56 saw stronger demand from those funds and five saw weaker demand. For business credit intermediaries, eight of 56 saw stronger demand and two saw weaker demand. Banks with rising nonbank demand pointed to working capital or liquidity, financial investment opportunities and refinancing. Banks that tightened cited an uncertain outlook and weaker borrower finances. The foreign panel also saw stronger demand from private equity funds. A tighter bank-to-fund link can therefore coincide with greater requests for liquidity from the fund, even while banks report fewer requests for loans from nonfinancial businesses. The published responses cannot trace a particular borrower or dollar through this chain.

questions.question: How much of the decline in domestic business-loan demand represents lower investment rather than lenders losing customers?
questions.detail: Compare the July-to-October reversal in domestic demand with the foreign panel’s stronger demand, then examine borrowing across lenders for the same firms. Banks’ conditional responses about equipment purchases and alternative funding establish two plausible mechanisms. A test needs firm investment and total finance alongside lender-specific balances to distinguish abandoned projects from financing that migrated.

questions.question: Did stricter lending standards constrain commercial-property projects that still sought credit?
questions.detail: Start with the separate construction, nonfarm nonresidential and multifamily balances. Match applications, approval rates and contract terms within each category to the same quarter. A decrease in applications and lower approval conditional on applying carry different implications. The published net balances document both pressures but reveal neither the rejected volume nor which borrowers stopped applying.

questions.question: Does greater private-equity demand represent liquidity insurance, refinancing or investment?
questions.detail: The special questions identify all three motives among banks experiencing stronger nonbank demand, without assigning each answer to a particular fund. Compare new commitments with drawdowns, refinancing schedules and acquisition financing in subsequent loan records. Use the number of banks answering each question and preserve the difference between a fund securing a line and actually drawing cash.

questions.question: Which cardholders faced the effective tightening?
questions.detail: Track approvals, credit limits and balances by risk group and bank size, retaining the distinction between non-originators and lenders that actively reduced approval likelihood. The evidence combines a year-long question on approvals with a quarterly question on demand. Align those windows before relating the responses to changes in spending, balances or delinquency.

limitation: This is a diffusion survey of bank officers. Different questions have different respondents and recall periods. The release does not identify loan amounts, individual borrower outcomes, a monetary-policy decision or a market reaction.
